To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) test case minimization is an effective technique for reducing the size of test sets while keeping block coverage the same; (ii) test sets with a fixed size are more effective than test sets with a constant coverage in terms of the number of detected faults and the number of undetected faults; (iii) test sets that are generated using the minimization technique are more effective than those generated without it in terms of the size/effectiveness trade-off.
the size of a block minimized test set is significantly reduced, while the fault detection effectiveness is almost the same as that of the non-minimized test set.

the size/effectiveness ratio of block minimized test sets, with respect to a constant block coverage, is better than the corresponding ratio of the original non-minimizing test sets, and that the size/effective ratio is independent of whether a test set is with respect to a fix size or a fix coverage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of test set minimization on fault detection effectiveness.
the following question: Can the size of a software test set be reduced while maintaining its fault detection effectiveness?
the effect of applying test set minimization techniques, which reduce the size of test sets, on the fault-detection effectiveness of the resulting test set.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
test case minimization can be a viable technique to reduce test set size, without sacrificing the fault detection effectiveness of the original test set.

, for the given application, the use of block test case minimization is a reasonable and effective approach to reduce test set size, without sacrificing fault detection effectiveness, and thus is a worthwhile endeavor.
the use of block coverage-based criteria as an effective test case selection criterion for reducing the size of test sets can be considered as a viable approach in practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in terms of the fault detection effectiveness, it is reasonable to use a block minimization technique to reduce the size, by up to 40 percent, of the test set, while still maintaining the same level of fault detection effectiveness.

test set minimization can be applied to reduce the size, and hence the cost, of a test set while keeping its fault detection effectiveness almost constant, if the test set was initially generated with respect to a coverage criterion.
the use of block minimization technique can reduce the size of test set without compromising its effectiveness.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for block coverage-based testing, it is possible to significantly minimize the size of test sets, while maintaining the fault detection effectiveness, and that the minimization can be achieved without any test case selection or test case screening.
test case screening during test set generation can be avoided and the resulting minimized test sets can be used to detect the majority of faults in software.
, if a test set is to be reduced in size, then block coverage should be used as a criterion for test case screening.
